questions.q: In the lesson's simulation, ads and sales had r = 0.819 even though ads had no effect on sales. What explains the correlation?
options: Ads cause sales, but weakly
Sales cause ads
The season, a confounder, influences both ad spend and sales
The p-value was too small to be reliable
questions.explain: A confounder drives both variables, creating a strong correlation with no direct causal link between them.

questions.q: What does a Pearson correlation of r = 0.02 between x and y tell you?
options: x and y are unrelated in every way
There is no straight-line association, but a curved relationship such as a U shape could still exist
x causes y very weakly
The data must contain an error
questions.explain: r measures linear association only. In the lesson, y was almost determined by x squared, yet r was about -0.165.

questions.q: Why does randomly assigning ad spend remove the confounding between ads and sales?
options: Random values are always larger
It makes the sample size bigger
It guarantees a significant p-value
Randomly assigned spend can't systematically track the season or any other hidden factor, so those factors no longer line up with it
questions.explain: Random assignment breaks the link between the treatment and every other variable, measured or not, on average. That is why randomized experiments are the standard for causal claims.

questions.q: Weeks with more sales show higher ad spend because managers boost the ad budget when sales are already rising. Which explanation is this?
options: Coincidence
Reverse causation (Y causes X)
Confounding by a third variable
X causes Y
questions.explain: Here the direction is flipped: the outcome (sales) influences the supposed cause (ad spend).

questions.q: You adjusted for season and the ads/sales correlation dropped to 0.009. What is the main limitation of this kind of adjustment?
options: It only accounts for confounders you thought of and measured; unmeasured ones remain
It always makes correlations zero
It cannot be done in Python
It proves that ads cause sales
questions.explain: Statistical adjustment handles measured confounders only, which is why randomization is stronger evidence for cause.
